planting.note: Divide and pot rhizome sections in spring into a loose, humus-rich, well-drained terrarium or woodland mix; keep in high humidity and bright shade year-round.

directions: Goodyera foliosa is a creeping terrestrial orchid from Himalayan and East Asian forests, spreading by a thin rhizome into loose colonies of small rosettes with broadly oval, dark green leaves marked by a pale central vein. In fall it sends up a short, glandular-hairy flower spike carrying a dozen or more small, greenish-white blooms, modest compared to showier orchids but charming set against the patterned foliage. Grow it the way jewel-orchid collectors grow its Asian relatives: in a loose, humus-rich, well-drained mix kept constantly moist, with high humidity and bright shade rather than direct sun. Where winters are cold it is best grown in a terrarium or cool greenhouse rather than left outdoors, since it has little tolerance for hard freezes.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Divide the creeping rhizome in spring and pot sections into a loose, free-draining, humus-rich terrarium mix; keep constantly moist and humid in bright shade.

directions: Goodyera hispida is a small East Asian terrestrial orchid grown chiefly for its reddish-brown, densely hairy leaves, a texture and color unusual among jewel orchids that otherwise tend toward smooth, silver-veined foliage. It forms low clumps of these velvety rosettes on a creeping rhizome across the humid forest floor of subtropical montane habitats in Taiwan and southern China, and responds in cultivation to the same conditions used for Goodyera velutina and other terrarium jewel orchids: constant moisture, high humidity, and bright shade with no direct sun. Small white flowers appear on a short spike but are secondary to the foliage, which is the main reason collectors seek the species out. Keep it in a loose, free-draining, humus-rich mix and propagate by dividing the creeping rhizome once a pot fills in.
sources: Taiwan Forestry Research Institute — Native Orchid Flora

planting.note: Divide and plant rhizome sections in early spring just as new shoots emerge, into reliably moist to boggy, humus-rich soil at a streamside or bog garden edge.

directions: Epipactis veratrifolia grows along streambanks and wet seepage slopes from the eastern Mediterranean through Iran and Pakistan into the Himalaya and western China, forming clumps of broad, pleated leaves topped in late spring by tall spikes of unusually large flowers for the genus, with green sepals and a maroon-purple, boat-shaped lip. The flowers are notable for a rare trick among orchids: they generate warmth and release scent compounds that mimic aphid-infested foliage, luring in hoverflies that normally lay eggs near aphid colonies and incidentally pollinate the flower instead. Grow it the way you would its North American relative Epipactis gigantea, in reliably moist to boggy, humus-rich soil at a streamside or bog-garden edge in partial shade, where its running rhizomes will slowly form a colony. Divide congested clumps in early spring just as new shoots emerge.
sources: Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew — Plants of the World Online

planting.note: Plant dormant divisions shallowly in early spring with growing eyes just below the soil surface, in cool, humus-rich, consistently moist, acidic woodland soil.

directions: Cypripedium debile is the smallest and most delicate of the hardy Asian lady's slippers in general cultivation, rising only a few inches on a thin, wiry stem topped by a single pair of thin, pleated, heart-shaped leaves held out like a tiny open parasol beneath one small, nodding, translucent greenish-yellow flower veined and spotted in maroon-brown. Native to the deep shade of moist mountain forests in China, Japan, Korea, and Taiwan, it wants the same cool, humus-rich, consistently moist, acidic woodland soil favored by other temperate Asian Cypripedium species such as C. japonicum, but on a miniature scale suited to a shaded trough or the front of a woodland bed rather than a bold border planting. Because the slender rhizome and shoots are easily damaged, handle dormant divisions carefully and set them shallowly with the growing eyes just below the soil surface in early spring. Winter chill is beneficial, but prolonged waterlogging around the dormant crown is a greater risk to this species than cold itself.
sources: American Orchid Society — Cypripedium Culture Notes
